claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: When 'isolate' songs are used as tutor songs, after two generations birds sing normally again.
claims.source: However, when these 'isolate' songs are used as tutor songs, after two generations birds sing normally again, suggesting that an 'innate' preference filters what aspects of a tutor song are actually imitated (Fehér et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fehér et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Song imitation requires approximately 75 s total exposure to a tutor song on a single day.
claims.source: Song imitation requires remarkably little total exposure to a tutor song – approximately 75 s total on a single day is enough for a bird to remember a song, and subsequently practice and imitate it (Deshpande et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Deshpande et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Zebra finches are able to imitate songs of birds from other species, but when given a choice they prefer zebra finch songs.
claims.source: Zebra finches, like many songbird species, are able to imitate songs of birds from other species, but when given a choice they prefer zebra finch songs (Eales, 1987).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Eales, 1987.

claims.claim: Inherited genetic predispositions have a strong effect on the precise tempo at which a zebra finch sings its song.
claims.source: Furthermore, inherited genetic predispositions have a strong effect on both the precise tempo at which a zebra finch sings its song (Mets and Brainard, 2018), as well as the particular learning styles of individual birds (Mets and Brainard, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mets and Brainard, 2018.

claims.claim: Inherited genetic predispositions have a strong effect on the particular learning styles of individual birds.
claims.source: Furthermore, inherited genetic predispositions have a strong effect on both the precise tempo at which a zebra finch sings its song (Mets and Brainard, 2018), as well as the particular learning styles of individual birds (Mets and Brainard, 2019).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mets and Brainard, 2019.

claims.claim: In typical birds, neurons in HVC are initially only weakly coupled to a song, firing only at the onsets of syllables when birds are babbling subsong.
claims.source: In typical birds, neurons in HVC are initially only weakly coupled to a song, firing only at the onsets of syllables when birds are babbling subsong (Okubo et al., 2015), and HVC is not necessary for subsong production (Aronov et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Okubo et al., 2015 and Aronov et al., 2008.

claims.claim: HVC is not necessary for subsong production.
claims.source: In typical birds, neurons in HVC are initially only weakly coupled to a song, firing only at the onsets of syllables when birds are babbling subsong (Okubo et al., 2015), and HVC is not necessary for subsong production (Aronov et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Aronov et al., 2008.

claims.claim: As the song becomes more mature and repeatable, each HVC projection neuron fires at its own precise moment during the song.
claims.source: Then, as the song becomes more mature and repeatable, each HVC projection neuron fires at its own precise moment during the song, with neurons firing one after the other, together forming a stable sequence of neural firing that tiles the song (Okubo et al., 2015; Lynch et al., 2016; Picardo et al., 2016), in interplay with inhibitory neurons (Kosche et al., 2015; Vallentin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: HVC maturation has been modeled as an initially random network of neurons that, with the right training inputs and plasticity rules, assembles into a chain of sequentially connected neurons.
claims.source: This maturation process in HVC has been modeled as an initially random network of neurons that, with the right training inputs and plasticity rules, assembles into a chain of sequentially connected neurons (Buonomano, 2005; Jun and Jin, 2007; Fiete et al., 2010; Okubo et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Isolate song has a much less stable sequence of syllables and abnormally variable acoustic structure and timing compared to typical adult zebra finch songs.
claims.source: Compared to typical adult zebra finch songs, isolate song has a much less stable sequence of syllables and abnormally variable acoustic structure and timing (Fehér et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fehér et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Aspects of isolate songs resemble features of early babbling (subsong).
claims.source: In fact, aspects of isolate songs resemble features of early babbling (subsong).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of isolate song characteristics with known features of subsong.

claims.claim: The seqNMF algorithm reveals the existence of significant sequential activity in HVC of singing isolated birds.
claims.source: This technique reveals the existence of significant sequential activity in HVC of singing isolated birds (Figure 1B and C, data in C also presented in Mackevicius et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claims.claim: In isolated birds, the seqNMF factorization explained 27 ± 9% of the power in the neural data, with a sequenciness score of 0.55 ± 0.88.
claims.source: In these birds, the seqNMF factorization explained 27 ± 9% of the power in the neural data, with a sequenciness score of 0.55 ± 0.88 (mean ± standard deviation).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the seqNMF analysis of the neural data.

claims.claim: In typical adult HVC, 46% of the data is explained by the seqNMF factorization, with sequenciness score of 0.74.
claims.source: Here, 46% of the data is explained by the seqNMF factorization, with sequenciness score of 0.74.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the seqNMF analysis of typical adult HVC data.

claims.claim: Neurons in isolated birds participate at characteristic moments during the sequence.
claims.source: As in typical HVC sequences, neurons in isolated birds participate at characteristic moments during the sequence (Figure 1E), and many neurons participate in at least one sequence (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: Many neurons in isolated birds participate in at least one sequence.
claims.source: As in typical HVC sequences, neurons in isolated birds participate at characteristic moments during the sequence (Figure 1E), and many neurons participate in at least one sequence (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Neurons that participate in a sequence tend to fire at a majority of sequence occurrences.
claims.source: Neurons that participate in a sequence tend to fire at a majority of sequence occurrences (Figure 1G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: On average, 45.21 ± 7% of participating neurons' activity was specific to sequences.
claims.source: On average, 45.21 ± 7% of these neurons' activity was specific to sequences.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis of neural data.

claims.claim: Neural sequences are correlated with precisely timed song features in isolated birds' songs.
claims.source: Neural sequences are correlated with precisely timed song features in isolated birds' songs (Figure 1H1, song features calculated as in Tchernichovski et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H and analysis using methods from Tchernichovski et al., 2000.

claims.claim: Song locking in isolated birds was only on average 0.58 times as strong as in a typically tutored adult bird.
claims.source: Song locking in isolated birds was only on average 0.58 times as strong as in a typically tutored adult bird (Figure 1J).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claims.claim: In isolated birds, on average only 61% of each song bout is represented by a detected HVC sequence.
claims.source: Finally, in isolated birds, on average only 61% of each song bout is represented by a detected HVC sequence, substantially less than the complete sequence coverage found in typically tutored birds (Picardo et al., 2016; Lynch et al., 2016; Okubo et al., 2015; Figure 1K, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by data shown in Figure 1K and comparison to prior research.

claims.claim: HVC sequences in isolated birds are more strongly present than would be expected from per-neuron circularly shifted data.
claims.source: By each of these measures, HVC sequences in isolated birds are more strongly present than would be expected from per-neuron circularly shifted data (red lines in Figure 1F–K), but not as robust as sequences observed in typically tutored birds (red triangles in Figure 1F–K).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to control data shown in Figure 1F-K.

claims.claim: HVC sequences in isolated birds are not as robust as sequences observed in typically tutored birds.
claims.source: By each of these measures, HVC sequences in isolated birds are more strongly present than would be expected from per-neuron circularly shifted data (red lines in Figure 1F–K), but not as robust as sequences observed in typically tutored birds (red triangles in Figure 1F–K).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison to typical bird data shown in Figure 1F-K.

claims.claim: Neurons in isolated birds sometimes generated extended periods of continuous activity, especially during long syllables of variable duration.
claims.source: While HVC neurons generate only brief bursts of spikes in tutored birds, neurons in isolated birds sometimes generated extended periods of continuous activity, especially during long syllables of variable duration (Figure 1L, 7/8 birds exhibited multiple instances of persistent activity, coordinated across at least three neurons, and lasting at least 500 ms).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1L, with quantification across birds.

claims.claim: HVC sequences in isolated birds exhibit variable durations, often truncating at different points.
claims.source: In addition, HVC sequences in isolated birds exhibit variable durations, often truncating at different points (Figure 1L, 8/8 birds), producing syllables of highly variable duration.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 1L, with quantification across all birds.

claims.claim: Truncations in the middle of a syllable are very unusual in typically tutored birds.
claims.source: Such truncations in the middle of a syllable, as opposed to at stereotyped gaps between syllables, are very unusual in typically tutored birds (Cynx, 1990).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cynx, 1990.

claims.claim: Syllables in isolated birds may exhibit variable duration when their underlying HVC sequences are truncated at different points.
claims.source: For example, syllables in isolated birds may exhibit variable duration when their underlying HVC sequences are truncated at different points.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claims.claim: HVC sequences were found in 5 birds at ages 57–64 dph, prior to tutor exposure.
claims.source: We recorded in 5 birds at ages 57–64 dph, prior to tutor exposure, and found strong evidence for HVC sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: There was not a significant correlation between the age of the bird and any sequence features measured.
claims.source: There was not a significant correlation between the age of the bird and any sequence features we measured (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F, linear regression model, significance threshold p<0.5, compared to a constant model).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F.

claims.claim: The large bird-to-bird variability in sequence properties is not explained by age, and is likely due to inter-individual variability in developmental timecourses.
claims.source: Thus, the large (several fold) bird-to-bird variability in sequence properties (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-F) is not explained by age, and is likely due to inter-individual variability in developmental timecourses.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of age correlation and observed variability.

claims.claim: Half of the young isolated birds learned elements of their tutor song after tutoring around the critical period.
claims.source: Many of our young isolated birds were eventually tutored at an age around the critical period and we found that half of them learned elements of their tutor song, while the others developed fully isolated songs.
claims.evidence: This is a direct observation from the experimental results.

claims.claim: Birds were classified as learners if their song had an Imitation Score metric greater than 0.5.
claims.source: We classified birds as learners if their song had an Imitation Score metric (Mandelblat-Cerf and Fee, 2014) greater than 0.5.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological criterion used in the study, referencing a prior method.

claims.claim: The songs of non-learners remained highly variable and isolate-like even after tutoring.
claims.source: The songs of non-learners remained highly variable and isolate-like even after tutoring (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Learner birds developed a new syllable within a day or two after tutoring.
claims.source: In contrast, learner birds developed a new syllable within a day or two after tutoring, and ultimately sang typical adult songs, consisting of stereotyped motifs (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The new syllables in learner birds appeared to imitate elements of the tutor song.
claims.source: The new syllables appeared to imitate elements of the tutor song, and persist as part of the learned song (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4.

claims.claim: Learner birds had fewer sequences than non-learners prior to tutoring.
claims.source: Learner birds had fewer sequences than non-learners (Figure 2C, average two sequences in learners, 3.25 sequences in non-learners, p=0.029, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical significance, shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Sequences in learner birds were more weakly correlated to song features than in non-learners.
claims.source: Sequences in learner birds were more weakly correlated to song features (Figure 2D, average 0.20 s learner, 0.55 s non-learner, p=0.0034, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical significance, shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Sequences in learners had lower autocorrelation than non-learners.
claims.source: Sequences in learners had lower autocorrelation, a measure of how repeatably/rhythmically they are produced (Okubo et al., 2015), than non-learners (Figure 2E, average 0.125 s learner, 0.244 s non-learner, p=0.018, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison with statistical significance, shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The age of tutoring did not significantly influence whether the bird was a learner or non-learner.
claims.source: In our dataset, the age of tutoring did not significantly influence whether the bird was a learner or non-learner (Figure 2F, average 60.5 dph learner, 78.75 dph non-learner, p=0.11, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The presence of robust song-locked sequences at the time of tutoring may inhibit learning.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that the presence, at the time of tutoring, of robust song-locked sequences, may inhibit learning.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of sequence properties between learners and non-learners.

claims.claim: Learning may be better supported by more immature sequences that are more independent from the vocal output.
claims.source: In other words, learning may be better supported by more immature sequences that are more independent from the vocal output.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed correlation between sequence maturity and learning ability.

claims.claim: Late-tutored birds that learned developed a new syllable within a day or two after tutoring.
claims.source: In late-tutored birds that learned, the speed with which new syllables appeared was striking. These birds developed a new syllable within a day or two after tutoring (Figure 2A and B), as has been previously described (Tchernichovski et al., 2001; Lipkind and Tchernichovski, 2011; Lipkind et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an observation supported by data in Figure 2A and B and citations to prior work.

claims.claim: New syllables in late-tutored learners appeared to emerge de-novo, not by syllable differentiation.
claims.source: These new syllables appeared to emerge de-novo, not by syllable differentiation as is common in tutored birds.
claims.evidence: This is an observation and interpretation of the data, contrasting with typical development.

claims.claim: Neural sequences associated with new post-tutoring syllables existed even prior to tutoring.
claims.source: We first extracted neural sequences associated with new post-tutoring syllables, then followed these neurons back in time to find that the sequence existed even prior to tutoring (Figure 3B and C, see Methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from tracking neurons across time, shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: In all four learner birds, the correlation between the pre-tutoring and post-tutoring sequences was significantly higher than expected by a time-shuffled control.
claims.source: In all four learner birds, the correlation between the pre-tutoring and post-tutoring sequences was significantly higher than expected by a time-shuffled control (p=0.014, p=0.018, p=0.0004, p=0.0002, respectively).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing to control data.

claims.claim: The correlation between pre- and post-tutoring sequences was significantly higher than a neuron-shuffled control in two birds.
claims.source: Additionally, the correlation between pre- and post- tutoring sequences was significantly higher than a neuron-shuffled control in two birds (p=0.0099, p=0.0032), and trended higher in the remaining two birds (p=0.077, p=0.079, likely influenced by an abundance of near-synchronous neurons, Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result comparing to control data, shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The sequences prior to tutoring were relatively uncoupled to vocal output, without a strong correlation to song syllables.
claims.source: Interestingly, the sequences prior to tutoring were relatively uncoupled to vocal output, without a strong correlation to song syllables.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of pre-tutoring sequences.

claims.claim: Neural sequences extracted two days after tutoring appeared to become more song locked after tutoring.
claims.source: Combining data from the four birds that learned a new syllable rapidly after tutoring, neural sequences extracted two days after tutoring appeared to become more song locked after tutoring (Figure 3D, p=0.0048, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: HVC sequences may exist in a 'latent' state in late-tutored birds prior to tutoring.
claims.source: This lack of coupling between HVC sequences and song structure prior to tutoring, and their subsequent incorporation into learned syllables, suggests that, in these late-tutored birds, HVC sequences may exist in a 'latent' state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the observed data.

claims.claim: Sequences that were initially relatively 'latent' persisted, becoming progressively more correlated with vocal output.
claims.source: Sequences that were initially relatively 'latent' persisted, becoming progressively more correlated with vocal output, ultimately appearing to become locked to a new syllable (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from tracking sequences forward in time, shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Each of the 'learner' birds appeared to have two HVC sequences present prior to tutoring.
claims.source: Each of the 'learner' birds appeared to have two HVC sequences present prior to tutoring.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the analysis of pre-tutoring data.

claims.claim: Pre-tutoring sequences that started off less correlated with song amplitude exhibited a significant increase in correlation with song amplitude after tutoring.
claims.source: Of these sequences, the ones that started off less correlated with song amplitude exhibited a significant increase in correlation with song amplitude after tutoring (Figure 3F, p=0.045, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Pre-tutoring sequences that started off more correlated with song amplitude did not significantly change their correlation with song amplitude after tutoring.
claims.source: The sequences that started off more correlated with song amplitude did not significantly change their correlation with song amplitude (Figure 3G, p=1, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: The emergence of new syllables after tutoring may co-opt existing HVC sequences, including relatively 'latent' sequences.
claims.source: Together, these results are consistent with the view that the emergence of new syllables after tutoring may co-opt existing HVC sequences, including relatively 'latent' sequences.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the observed data.

claims.claim: HVC network activity can form long repeatable sequences even in birds that had no prior exposure to vocal tutoring.
claims.source: By observing the neural activity in HVC of isolated birds, we found that HVC network activity can form long repeatable sequences even in birds that had no prior exposure to vocal tutoring.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the primary finding from the study.

claims.claim: Sequences in isolate HVC exhibit some properties of typical HVC, with many neurons reliably participating in sequences, and sequences being correlated to vocal output.
claims.source: Sequences in isolate HVC exhibit some properties of typical HVC, with many neurons reliably participating in sequences, and sequences being correlated to vocal output.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the comparison of isolate and typical HVC.

claims.claim: Sequences in isolated birds were less reliable and less tightly correlated with vocal output than has been described in typical birds.
claims.source: However, sequences in isolated birds were less reliable and less tightly correlated with vocal output than has been described in typical birds, and exhibited abnormal truncations and persistent activity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the comparison of isolate and typical HVC.

claims.claim: There must be a way for sequences to form without the prior storage of a tutor memory.
claims.source: We had previously hypothesized that the experience of hearing a tutor may seed the formation of HVC sequences of the appropriate number and durations (Mackevicius and Fee, 2018), but our new data reveal that HVC sequences exist even prior to tutoring. Thus, there must be a way for sequences to form without the prior storage of a tutor memory.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding that sequences exist prior to tutoring.

claims.claim: In models of Hebbian learning in HVC, sequences can form in networks driven by random inputs rather than patterned inputs.
claims.source: In models of Hebbian learning in HVC, sequences can form in networks driven by random inputs rather than patterned inputs (Fiete et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fiete et al., 2010.

claims.claim: When sequences form from random inputs, the distribution of sequence durations no longer matches syllable durations found in typical adult birds, but is instead more consistent with the highly variable and atypically long syllables that occur in isolate song.
claims.source: However, in this case, the distribution of sequence durations no longer matches syllable durations found in typical adult birds, but is instead more consistent with the highly variable and atypically long syllables that occur in birds that have never heard a tutor (isolate song) (Fehér et al., 2009; Price, 1979).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from modeling results and comparison to isolate song characteristics, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Sequences can emerge in isolate birds by a combination of simple Hebbian learning mechanisms together with spontaneous activity either within HVC or driven by the inputs to HVC.
claims.source: Thus our findings are consistent with the view that sequences can emerge in isolate birds by a combination of simple Hebbian learning mechanisms together with spontaneous activity either within HVC or driven by the inputs to HVC.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the findings and modeling considerations.

claims.claim: The discovery of latent sequences suggests a separation between neural processes for building a stable representation of states within a task and neural processes for associating an action with each state.
claims.source: Our discovery of latent sequences suggests a separation between neural processes for building a stable representation of states within a task (i.e. sequential moments in time), and neural processes for associating an action with each state.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation and inference from the discovery of latent sequences.

claims.claim: Sequences may gradually emerge in the maturing HVC network via simple Hebbian processes, but may remain relatively decoupled from downstream motor neurons until a memory of the tutor song is learned and reinforcement learning processes begin.
claims.source: Thus, sequences may gradually emerge in the maturing HVC network via simple Hebbian processes (Buonomano, 2005; Jun and Jin, 2007; Fiete et al., 2010; Okubo et al., 2015), but may remain relatively decoupled from downstream motor neurons until a memory of the tutor song is learned and reinforcement learning processes begin.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation and speculation based on the findings and cited models.

claims.claim: In reinforcement learning models of song learning, HVC sequences remain relatively stable even as the song changes.
claims.source: In reinforcement learning models of song learning, HVC sequences remain relatively stable even as the song changes (Doya and Sejnowski, 1994; Fiete et al., 2007; Fee and Goldberg, 2011; Brainard and Doupe, 2013), consistent with our observation of stable sequences.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior models and is consistent with the observed data.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with data from the primary motor cortex of macaques operating a brain-computer interface—a fixed repertoire of activity patterns is associated with different movements after learning.
claims.source: Our results are consistent with data from the primary motor cortex of macaques operating a brain-computer interface—a fixed repertoire of activity patterns is associated with different movements after learning (Golub et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement draws a parallel to findings in another system, supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The results are consistent with the idea that the brain may use pre-existing sequential patterns to rapidly learn from new experiences.
claims.source: Our results are also consistent with the idea that the brain may use pre-existing sequential patterns to rapidly learn from new experiences, for example, the existence of sequences in the hippocampus prior to exposure to new environments (Villette et al., 2015; Farooq et al., 2019; McKenzie et al., 2021; Dragoi, 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement draws a parallel to findings in the hippocampus, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Zebra finches develop typical songs, including typical syllable durations, after being tutored by atypical isolate songs, relying on species-specific 'priors'.
claims.source: Zebra finches are known to develop typical songs, including typical syllable durations, after being tutored by atypical isolate songs, relying on species-specific 'priors' to achieve species-typical syllable durations.
claims.evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about zebra finch song learning.

claims.claim: The latent sequences observed tended to last approximately a couple hundred milliseconds—the same as the duration of typical zebra finch syllables.
claims.source: The latent sequences we observed tended to last approximately a couple hundred milliseconds—the same as the duration of typical zebra finch syllables.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claims.claim: The speed of latent sequences could be genetically specified by expression levels of ion channels with different time constants within HVC.
claims.source: One might imagine that the speed of latent sequences could be genetically specified by expression levels of ion channels with different time constants within HVC.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the mechanism underlying latent sequence timing.

claims.claim: The duration of latent sequences could be specified by the amount of time it takes for HVC to get feedback from respiratory and/or auditory centers.
claims.source: Alternatively, the duration of latent sequences could be specified by the amount of time it takes for HVC to get feedback from respiratory and/or auditory centers, which may also have their own intrinsic timing or rhythmicity (Schmidt and Goller, 2016; Hamaguchi et al., 2016; Araki et al., 2016; Mackevicius et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by citations to prior work on feedback mechanisms.

claims.claim: Latent sequences appear to be capable of supporting song learning, at least in the case of delayed tutoring.
claims.source: By whatever mechanism latent sequences arise, they appear to be capable of supporting song learning, at least in the case of delayed tutoring.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observed data showing that latent sequences become associated with learned syllables.

claims.claim: The ability of brains to generate complex learned behavior may depend on the intrinsic developmental formation of appropriate latent dynamics in motor and sensory circuits.
claims.source: More generally, the ability of brains to generate complex learned behavior may depend on the intrinsic developmental formation of appropriate latent dynamics in motor and sensory circuits.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative generalization from the findings.

claims.claim: Eight birds were foster-raised by female birds starting on or before post-hatch day 15.
claims.source: In order to control exposure to a tutor song, eight birds were foster-raised by female birds, which do not sing, starting on or before post-hatch day 15 (15 dph).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claims.claim: Starting between 35 dph and 50 dph, birds were housed singly in custom-made sound isolation chambers.
claims.source: Starting between 35 dph and 50 dph, these birds were housed singly in custom-made sound isolation chambers.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claims.claim: The calcium indicator GCaMP6f was expressed in HVC by intercranial injection of the viral vector AAV9.CAG.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40.
claims.source: The calcium indicator GCaMP6f was expressed in HVC by intercranial injection of the viral vector AAV9.CAG.GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 (Chen et al., 2013) into HVC.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods, with citation to the viral vector source.

claims.claim: Most if not all of the neurons included in the datasets are likely to be projection neurons, not HVC interneurons.
claims.source: It is not known whether this virus is specific to projection neurons in HVC. However, given the dense firing patterns of HVC interneurons, once convolved with the GCaMP6f calcium kernel, HVC interneuron activity would likely look flat, almost indistinguishable from the background. Therefore, in practice, most if not all of the neurons included in our datasets are likely to be projection neurons, not HVC interneurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of HVC interneurons and the calcium imaging method.

claims.claim: Neuronal activity traces were extracted from raw fluorescence movies using CNMF_E algorithm.
claims.source: Neuronal activity traces were extracted from raw fluorescence movies using a constrained non-negative matrix factorization algorithm, CNMF_E, that is specialized for microendoscope data by including a local background model to remove activity from out-of-focus cells (Zhou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods, with citation to the algorithm.

claims.claim: SeqNMF measures the extent to which a dataset contains sequential vs. synchronous patterns using a 'sequenciness' score, which ranges between 0 and 1.
claims.source: SeqNMF measures the extent to which a dataset contains sequential vs. synchronous patterns using a 'sequenciness' score, which ranges between 0 and 1. A score of zero indicates that all explanatory power of the factorization is due to synchronous activity, while a score of one indicates that none of the explanatory power is due to synchronous activity.
claims.evidence: This is a description of a metric from the seqNMF algorithm.

claims.claim: Birds isolated from a tutor are able to learn a song if exposed to a tutor before the end of a critical period, typically around age 65 days post-hatch.
claims.source: Birds isolated from a tutor are able to learn a song if exposed to a tutor before the end of a critical period, typically around age 65 days post-hatch (dph), but are increasingly unable to learn at later ages (London, 2019; Gobes et al., 2019; Immelmann, 1969).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

results.result: HVC neural sequences exist in isolated birds without tutor exposure, but these sequences are less robust than in typically tutored birds. The seqNMF algorithm revealed sequential activity in isolated birds (27±9% variance explained, sequenciness 0.55±0.88) compared to typical adults (46% variance, sequenciness 0.74). While many neurons participate reliably in sequences and correlate with vocal output, isolated bird sequences show weaker song locking (0.58× typical strength), cover only 61% of song bouts, and are less robust than typical sequences but stronger than shuffled controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C26-C37, C71-C73 collectively demonstrate that neural sequences form without tutoring using calcium imaging and seqNMF analysis (Figures 1B-K). Quantitative metrics with appropriate controls (circular shift, typical bird comparisons) support the conclusion that sequences exist but are atypical. Statistical comparisons are provided for key measures.

results.result: Isolated bird HVC sequences exhibit abnormal features including extended persistent activity (7/8 birds) and variable-duration truncations (8/8 birds), contrasting with the brief bursts typical of tutored birds. These abnormalities may explain characteristic isolate song features like abnormally long and variable-duration syllables.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 describe qualitative differences in isolated HVC with quantification across birds (Figure 1L). The persistent activity and truncations are documented observations, though the mechanistic link to syllable variability (C41) is speculative but reasonable given the data.

results.result: HVC sequences are present in young isolated birds (57-64 dph) prior to the critical period, with no significant correlation between age and sequence features. The large inter-bird variability in sequence properties is attributed to individual differences in developmental timecourses rather than age.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C44-C45 are supported by data from 5 birds showing sequences before tutoring (Figure 1—supplement 1A) and regression analysis finding no age correlation (p>0.5, Figure 1—supplement 1B-F). The inference about individual variability (C45) is reasonable given the lack of age effect.

results.result: Half of late-tutored isolated birds learned new syllables (Imitation Score >0.5) while others remained isolate-like. Learners had fewer sequences (2 vs 3.25, p=0.029), weaker song correlation (0.20 vs 0.55, p=0.0034), and lower autocorrelation (0.125 vs 0.244, p=0.018) than non-learners prior to tutoring. Age of tutoring did not significantly predict learning outcome (p=0.11).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C46-C54 present a clear pattern with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank sum) and visual data (Figure 2). The classification criterion (C47) is methodologically sound. Sample sizes are small (n=4 learners, n=4 non-learners) but statistical significance is achieved for key measures.

results.result: The presence of robust, song-locked HVC sequences at the time of tutoring may inhibit learning, while more immature sequences that are decoupled from vocal output may better support learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 are inferences from the quantitative differences between learners and non-learners (C51-C53). The correlation between sequence maturity and learning failure is well-supported by the data, making this a reasonable mechanistic interpretation, though causality is not definitively established.

results.result: In late-tutored learners, new syllables emerged within 1-2 days and appeared de-novo rather than by differentiation. Neural sequences associated with these new syllables existed prior to tutoring but were weakly coupled to vocal output. After tutoring, these pre-existing sequences became significantly more song-locked (p=0.0048) and correlated with the new syllables.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C64 describe tracking sequences across tutoring using neuron tracking methods (Figure 3A-D). Statistical tests with appropriate controls (time-shuffled, neuron-shuffled) support sequence persistence (C61-C62). The observation of increased song locking (C64) is statistically significant. The de-novo appearance claim (C58) is observational but reasonable.

results.result: HVC sequences may exist in a 'latent' state prior to tutoring—present but weakly coupled to vocal output. Learner birds had two pre-tutoring sequences; those initially less correlated with song amplitude showed significant increases after tutoring (p=0.045), while initially stronger sequences did not change (p=1). This suggests new syllables co-opt existing latent sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 extend the tracking analysis (Figure 3E-G) with appropriate statistical tests. The 'latent sequence' concept (C65, C70) is an interpretation well-supported by the differential changes in song locking for weak vs. strong pre-tutoring sequences (C68-C69). The observation of two sequences per bird (C67) is consistent across learners.

results.result: Sequences can form without prior tutor memory storage. Modeling work shows Hebbian learning with random inputs can generate sequences, though with durations matching variable isolate syllables rather than typical syllables. The findings are consistent with sequences emerging via Hebbian mechanisms and spontaneous HVC activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 integrate the empirical findings with computational models. C74 is a logical inference from C4. C75-C76 appropriately cite modeling work (Fiete et al., 2010) and connect predictions to observed isolate song features. C77 is a reasonable synthesis, though speculative.

results.result: The discovery of latent sequences suggests separation between building sequential state representations and associating actions with states. This is consistent with reinforcement learning models where HVC sequences remain stable during song changes, and parallels findings in motor cortex (brain-computer interface) and hippocampus (pre-existing place sequences).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 place findings in broader theoretical context. C78-C79 are reasonable interpretations of the latent sequence data. C80-C82 appropriately cite supporting work from other systems, strengthening the generalizability of the findings. The parallels drawn are conceptually sound.

results.result: Latent sequences lasted ~200ms, matching typical zebra finch syllable durations, suggesting species-specific timing may be genetically specified (via ion channel expression or feedback timing). These latent sequences appear capable of supporting delayed-tutoring learning, potentially representing a general mechanism for rapid learning from sparse data.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C88 mix observations (C84) with speculation (C85-C86, C88). While C84 is a data observation and C87 is supported by the learning results, the mechanistic hypotheses (C85-C86) are untested speculations. The generalization (C88) is interesting but highly speculative without additional evidence from other systems or species.

results.result: Methods: Birds were foster-raised by females from ≤15 dph, isolated 35-50 dph. GCaMP6f was expressed via AAV9 injection. Neurons were extracted using CNMF_E algorithm. Most recorded neurons are likely projection neurons, not interneurons. SeqNMF algorithm measures sequential vs. synchronous patterns via 'sequenciness' score (0-1).
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93, C95 describe experimental and analytical methods with appropriate citations. The inference about neuron types (C92) is reasonable given interneuron firing properties and calcium imaging limitations. Methods are sufficiently detailed and use established, validated approaches.

results.result: Background context: Behaviors emerge from experience and innate predispositions. Brain development involves both sensory experience and genetic processes. In songbirds, learning is influenced by tutor exposure and inherited preferences. Isolate birds develop atypical songs. HVC neurons mature from weakly coupled (subsong) to forming precise sequences in typical development. Critical period for learning typically ends ~65 dph.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C8-C25, C96 provide established background knowledge, all supported by appropriate citations to prior literature. These contextual claims accurately represent the field's understanding and properly frame the current study's questions.
